name: Cervical Radiculopathy
summary: Cervical nerve-root disorder causing neck/arm pain with sensory, motor or reflex changes in a root distribution.

firstSteps: Repeated or directional movement when clearly beneficial
selfCare: Frequent gentle movement rather than bed rest

assess: Spurling/distraction and upper-limb neurodynamic tests where appropriate

tests.name: Spurling Test
tests.purpose: Reproduce nerve-root symptoms with foraminal compression.
tests.positive: Reproduction of familiar radiating arm pain/paresthesia, not just local neck discomfort.

tests.name: Cervical Distraction Test
tests.purpose: Assess whether unloading the nerve root reduces symptoms.
tests.positive: Reduction of familiar radicular arm symptoms.

tests.name: Upper Limb Neurodynamic Test — Median Bias
tests.positive: Familiar neural symptoms reproduced and modified by structural differentiation.

stages.label: Symptom Reduction & Neurologic Monitoring
stages.goal: Reduce arm symptoms and maintain safe movement.
do: Repeated or directional movement when clearly beneficial
dose: Neck ROM/repeated movement: small sets of 5–10 based on directional response

stages.label: Mobility & Strength
stages.goal: Restore cervical/scapular capacity and functional tolerance.

stages.label: Return to Demands
stages.goal: Restore work/sport lifting and sustained postures.

logic: Confirm whether symptoms behave like a cervical nerve-root problem rather than shoulder pathology, peripheral nerve entrapment or myelopathy.
Neurological status is more important than pain intensity alone. Track myotomes, dermatomes and reflexes over time.
Centralization or reduction of distal arm symptoms is generally a favorable response; repeated peripheralization is a warning to change the intervention.
classification: Root level based on neurologic distribution
investigations: MRI is considered for progressive neurologic deficit, red flags or persistent severe symptoms when results will change management.
Electrodiagnostic testing can help when peripheral nerve vs root localization is uncertain.
manual: Cervical/thoracic mobilization and traction may be used in selected patients as part of a multimodal program.
Avoid high-risk manipulation when vascular, instability, myelopathy or other contraindications are suspected.
Thoracic or cervical mobilization when tolerated
Gentle traction as a symptom-response test
Avoid aggressive end-range techniques during high irritability
Gentle cervical or thoracic mobilization can be used if it reduces arm symptoms or improves motion.
Manual traction can be tested with a low force first; continue only if symptoms ease or centralize.
Neurodynamic sliders are preferred before tensioners in irritable cases.
Avoid aggressive end-range cervical techniques when neurological symptoms are easily provoked.
modalities: Traction may reduce symptoms in selected cases.
Heat/TENS may provide temporary comfort but should not replace neurologic monitoring and active rehabilitation.
Short-term heat or TENS may be used for comfort
Traction is considered only when the patient shows a favorable response; it is not automatically required
Heat or TENS can be used for short-term comfort but should not be the main intervention.
Traction is not automatically indicated by the diagnosis; dose it only in clear responders.
dosing: Pain-free cervical repeated movement in the helpful direction: 5–10 repetitions, repeated several times/day if it centralizes symptoms.
Median/ulnar/radial nerve sliders: usually 10–20 gentle repetitions × 1–3 sets/day without prolonged distal tingling.
Deep neck flexor and scapular endurance: 2–3 sets of low-load controlled work.
Progress upper-limb strengthening from light resistance to normal functional loading once neurological irritability is stable.
progression: Progress from symptom control to endurance and loaded upper-quarter tasks
Increase neural excursion only when distal symptoms remain stable or improve
Progress when distal symptoms are less frequent/intense and strength is stable or improving.
Move from sliders to greater neural excursion gradually.
Return to lifting/overhead tasks only after the patient can load the arm without progressive paresthesia or weakness.
mistakes: Calling any arm pain radiculopathy without neurologic exam
Continuing an exercise that repeatedly pushes symptoms farther down the arm.
Assuming every arm symptom is radiculopathy.
Using traction for long periods without checking whether it actually changes symptoms.
pearls: Spurling may reproduce familiar arm symptoms and distraction may relieve them; neither finding alone establishes the diagnosis.
Progressive motor loss changes the urgency of management.
Record myotomes, dermatomes, reflexes and functional change at baseline and follow-up; a single provocative test should not establish the diagnosis.
Progressive weakness, signs of spinal cord involvement, gait/balance change, bilateral neurological symptoms or bowel/bladder disturbance require urgent medical assessment.
Use symptom response and neurological status to guide exercise and manual therapy; do not repeatedly provoke distal symptoms to demonstrate a positive test.
If symptoms or examination findings suggest peripheral nerve or shoulder pathology, revisit the differential rather than anchoring on a cervical source.
education: Teach the difference between local neck soreness and worsening neurological symptoms.
Explain that movement is usually helpful when it does not progressively spread symptoms distally.
Advise urgent review for progressive weakness, gait changes, hand clumsiness or bowel/bladder changes.
escalation: Urgent referral for progressive weakness, myelopathy or major neurological deterioration
Medical review when severe disabling symptoms persist despite appropriate conservative care

tests.name: Spurling Test
tests.purpose: Reproduce nerve-root symptoms with foraminal compression.
tests.positive: Reproduction of familiar radiating arm pain/paresthesia, not just local neck discomfort.
tests.handPlacement: Hands over head to guide position and apply gentle axial load.
procedure: Side-bend/rotate toward the symptomatic side as clinically appropriate.
Stop immediately if severe symptoms occur.
tests.interpretation: Supports cervical radiculopathy when combined with neurologic examination.

tests.name: Cervical Distraction Test
tests.purpose: Assess whether unloading the nerve root reduces symptoms.
tests.positive: Reduction of familiar radicular arm symptoms.
tests.therapistPosition: At the head of the patient.
procedure: Maintain briefly and reassess arm symptoms.

tests.name: Upper Limb Neurodynamic Test — Median Bias
tests.positive: Familiar neural symptoms reproduced and modified by structural differentiation.
tests.handPlacement: Control shoulder, elbow, forearm and wrist.
procedure: Externally rotate shoulder and gradually extend elbow.
Use cervical side-bending as a sensitizer if appropriate.
tests.interpretation: Supports neural mechanosensitivity; interpret with root/median nerve exam.

story.headline: The neck mystery that sent a message to the fingers
story.scene: A programmer arrives rubbing the shoulder but points to tingling in the thumb and index finger. 'The trouble is in my neck. Why are my fingers getting notifications?' It is time to follow the nerve pathway.
story.dialogue: Patient: 'Is my arm wiring faulty?' Therapist: 'Maybe irritated, not necessarily damaged. We'll check the entire circuit.'
story.clue: Neck-to-arm pain, dermatomal sensory changes, root-pattern weakness or reflex alteration may suggest cervical nerve-root involvement. Other peripheral nerve problems can imitate it.
story.twist: Tingling alone does not identify a root. Progressive weakness, gait disturbance or other myelopathy signs change the urgency of assessment.
story.aha: Where the symptom travels can be more revealing than where the patient first felt pain.
story.patientTranslation: A nerve coming from the neck may be irritated, which can cause arm pain, tingling or weakness. We'll examine strength, sensation, reflexes and warning signs before deciding on treatment.
story.clinicianReasoning: Perform neurologic screen, dermatomal/myotomal/reflex testing, assess cervical movement and provocative clusters when safe. Consider median nerve entrapment and shoulder referral. Escalate progressive motor loss or signs of cord involvement.
story.rehabBridge: First screen and calm symptoms → restore tolerable neck/upper-quarter movement → build strength, activity tolerance and a graded return to tasks.
story.question: A neck-pain patient develops progressive hand weakness and new gait imbalance. What should happen next?
options: Escalate urgently for possible neurologic/cord involvement
Reassure that all tingling is harmless
story.explanation: Progressive motor deficits and gait changes can indicate serious neurologic involvement and warrant urgent medical evaluation.
